title: Health
description: Free Health study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

concepts.intro: Mental health is not a fixed label of 'healthy' or 'ill' — it exists on a continuum from thriving to struggling, and everyone moves along it over time depending on life circumstances, coping skills, and support.
b: Mental health includes emotional, psychological, and social well-being, and affects how a person thinks, feels, and acts
Good mental health does not mean the absence of hard feelings; it means having the tools to cope with them
Risk factors (trauma, chronic stress, family history, substance use) push someone toward the struggling end
Protective factors (supportive relationships, sleep, exercise, coping skills, sense of purpose) push someone toward thriving
A person can have a diagnosed mental illness and still function well with treatment and support
Checking in on your own mental state regularly is a normal, healthy habit, not a sign of weakness

concepts.l: Stress and the Body's Stress Response
concepts.intro: Stress is the body's physical and emotional reaction to a demand or challenge. The 'fight-or-flight' response releases adrenaline and cortisol to prepare the body to react quickly, which is helpful short-term but harmful if triggered constantly.
b: Eustress is positive, motivating stress (like nervous excitement before a game); distress is negative stress that overwhelms coping ability
The fight-or-flight response increases heart rate, breathing rate, and blood sugar while diverting blood from digestion to muscles
Acute stress is short-term and resolves; chronic stress persists over weeks or months and wears down the body
Chronic stress is linked to headaches, high blood pressure, weakened immune function, sleep problems, and anxiety/depression
Common teen stressors include academic pressure, social relationships, family conflict, and social media comparison
Time management, physical activity, and talking to someone are proven ways to reduce the physical impact of stress

concepts.intro: Emotional intelligence (EQ) is the ability to recognize, understand, and manage your own emotions while also recognizing and responding well to the emotions of others.
b: Self-awareness means accurately naming what you feel and recognizing what triggers it
Self-management is choosing how to respond to an emotion rather than reacting impulsively
Empathy is the ability to understand and share another person's feelings without judgment
Social skills built on EQ include active listening, clear communication, and conflict resolution
All emotions (including anger, jealousy, sadness) are normal; it is the behavior that follows an emotion that can be healthy or unhealthy
Journaling, naming feelings out loud, and pausing before reacting all strengthen emotional intelligence over time

concepts.intro: Coping strategies are the specific actions people use to manage stress and difficult emotions. Resilience is the ability to adapt and bounce back after setbacks, and it can be built like a skill.
b: Healthy coping includes exercise, talking to a trusted person, deep breathing, creative outlets, and problem-solving
Unhealthy coping includes substance use, avoidance, self-harm, aggression, and social withdrawal — these provide short-term relief but worsen problems long-term
Resilience is built through supportive relationships, a growth mindset, realistic goal-setting, and practicing problem-solving under manageable stress
Cognitive reframing means changing how you interpret a stressful situation to reduce its emotional impact
A strong support network (family, friends, mentors, counselors) is one of the biggest predictors of resilience
Self-care — sleep, nutrition, physical activity, and downtime — is a foundation that makes all other coping strategies more effective

concepts.intro: Anxiety disorders and depression are the most common mental health conditions among teens. They are medical conditions involving changes in brain chemistry and function, not a choice or character flaw.
b: Generalized anxiety disorder involves excessive, hard-to-control worry most days for six months or more that interferes with daily life
Depression involves persistent sadness or loss of interest lasting two weeks or longer, along with changes in sleep, appetite, energy, or concentration
Both conditions have biological (brain chemistry, genetics), psychological, and environmental (stress, trauma) causes
Effective treatments include talk therapy (like cognitive behavioral therapy), medication, and lifestyle changes — often used in combination
Untreated anxiety and depression can affect school performance, relationships, and physical health
Stigma (negative stereotypes about mental illness) is a major reason people delay seeking treatment

concepts.intro: Knowing the warning signs of a mental health crisis and how to respond can save a life. Suicide is preventable, and most people who consider it give some warning signs beforehand.
b: Warning signs include talking about wanting to die, giving away belongings, sudden calmness after depression, withdrawing from others, and reckless behavior
If you notice these signs in a friend, tell a trusted adult immediately — this is not betraying a secret, it is protecting a life
Directly and calmly asking someone 'Are you thinking about suicide?' does not plant the idea; it opens the door to help
988 is the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in the U.S., available 24/7 by call, text, or chat
School counselors, trusted adults, doctors, and mental health professionals are all appropriate resources for getting help
Recovery is possible with the right support — most people with mental health conditions improve significantly with treatment

keyFacts: About 1 in 5 teens experiences a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year, most commonly anxiety or depression
Chronic (long-term) stress raises cortisol levels and is linked to high blood pressure, weakened immunity, and disrupted sleep
Depression is diagnosed when symptoms last two weeks or more and interfere with daily functioning, not just a bad day
988 (call, text, or chat) is the free, confidential U.S. Suicide & Crisis Lifeline available 24 hours a day
traps: All stress is harmful, not true — eustress (like excitement before a big game) is short-term stress that can improve focus and performance
Mental illness is a sign of personal weakness, not true — it is a medical condition involving brain chemistry, genetics, and environment, just like a physical illness
Asking someone directly if they're suicidal will give them the idea, not true — direct, caring questions open the door to help and do not increase risk
Keeping a friend's suicidal thoughts secret is loyalty, not true — telling a trusted adult immediately is the responsible, life-saving action

concepts.intro: Macronutrients are the nutrients the body needs in large amounts for energy and growth: carbohydrates, proteins, and fats. Each has a distinct job in the body.
b: Carbohydrates are the body's primary and preferred energy source, found in grains, fruits, vegetables, and legumes
Complex carbohydrates (whole grains, vegetables) digest slowly and provide steady energy; simple carbohydrates (sugar) digest quickly and spike blood sugar
Proteins build and repair tissue (including muscle) and are made of amino acids; sources include meat, fish, eggs, dairy, beans, and nuts
Fats provide long-term energy storage, support cell function, and help absorb fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)
Unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, avocado, fish) support heart health; saturated and trans fats, eaten in excess, raise heart disease risk
Each gram of carbohydrate or protein provides about 4 calories; each gram of fat provides about 9 calories

concepts.intro: Micronutrients are vitamins and minerals needed in small amounts that support essential body functions like immunity, bone health, and energy metabolism.
b: Vitamin C supports immune function and wound healing; found in citrus fruits, peppers, and broccoli
Calcium and vitamin D work together to build and maintain strong bones and teeth
Iron carries oxygen in the blood; a deficiency causes anemia, leading to fatigue and weakness
B vitamins help convert food into usable energy at the cellular level
Most micronutrient needs can be met through a varied diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins
Water-soluble vitamins (like C and B vitamins) are not stored well and need regular replenishment; fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in body fat

concepts.intro: MyPlate is the USDA's visual guide for building balanced meals, replacing the older food pyramid, and emphasizing portion balance across food groups.
b: MyPlate divides a plate into four sections: fruits, vegetables, grains, and protein, plus a side of dairy
Half the plate should be fruits and vegetables at most meals
Whole grains (brown rice, whole wheat bread, oats) are recommended over refined grains for more fiber and nutrients
Lean protein sources include poultry, fish, beans, eggs, and nuts
Portion control, not just food choice, matters for maintaining a healthy weight
Reading nutrition labels helps identify serving size, calories, added sugars, and sodium content

concepts.intro: Physical fitness has five key components, and a well-rounded fitness plan addresses all of them rather than just one.
b: Cardiorespiratory endurance is the heart and lungs' ability to supply oxygen during sustained activity (e.g., running, swimming)
Muscular strength is the maximum force a muscle can produce (e.g., lifting a heavy weight one time)
Muscular endurance is a muscle's ability to perform repeated contractions over time without fatigue (e.g., many push-ups)
Flexibility is the range of motion available at a joint, improved through stretching
Body composition is the ratio of fat mass to lean mass (muscle, bone, organs) in the body
The FITT principle (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type) is used to design an effective, individualized exercise plan

concepts.intro: Regular physical activity benefits nearly every body system and is one of the most powerful tools for long-term health, both physical and mental.
b: The CDC recommends teens get at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity every day
Aerobic exercise strengthens the heart and lungs and reduces risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity
Resistance/strength training builds muscle and bone density, which is especially important during adolescent growth
Exercise releases endorphins, improving mood and reducing symptoms of stress, anxiety, and depression
Regular activity improves sleep quality and helps regulate a healthy body weight
Both aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities should be included across a week for balanced fitness

concepts.l: Body Image, Eating Disorders, and Healthy Weight Management
concepts.intro: A healthy relationship with food and body image is essential; when it breaks down, it can lead to disordered eating patterns that require professional treatment.
b: Anorexia nervosa involves severe restriction of food intake driven by an intense fear of gaining weight and a distorted body image
Bulimia nervosa involves cycles of binge eating followed by purging (vomiting, laxatives, or excessive exercise)
Binge eating disorder involves recurrent episodes of eating large amounts of food with a feeling of loss of control, without purging
Eating disorders are serious mental illnesses with physical, psychological, and social causes — they are not simply about vanity
Healthy weight management focuses on balanced nutrition and regular activity, not extreme dieting or fasting
Media and social media images are often edited or filtered, contributing to unrealistic body standards

keyFacts: MyPlate recommends filling half the plate with fruits and vegetables at most meals
Carbohydrates and protein each provide about 4 calories per gram; fat provides about 9 calories per gram
The CDC recommends at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily for teens
The five components of fitness are cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility, and body composition
traps: 'Fat-free' means healthy, not true — fat-free foods often add sugar to make up for lost flavor, so the label alone doesn't guarantee it's healthier
Skipping meals is an effective way to lose weight, not true — it often leads to overeating later and can slow metabolism
Eating disorders are a lifestyle choice about vanity, not true — they are serious mental illnesses with biological, psychological, and social roots
All fats are bad for you, not true — unsaturated fats (nuts, olive oil, fish) support heart health, while saturated/trans fats in excess raise risk

concepts.l: Categories of Drugs and How They Affect the Body
concepts.intro: Drugs are classified by how they affect the central nervous system: depressants, stimulants, and hallucinogens each produce different effects on mood, perception, and body function.
b: Depressants (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines) slow down central nervous system activity, causing relaxation, slowed breathing, and impaired coordination
Stimulants (nicotine, cocaine, methamphetamine, excess caffeine) speed up the central nervous system, increasing heart rate, alertness, and blood pressure
Hallucinogens (LSD, psilocybin) alter perception, thoughts, and feelings, causing sensory distortions
Tolerance is needing more of a substance over time to get the same effect
Physical dependence occurs when the body adapts to a substance and experiences withdrawal symptoms without it
Addiction is a chronic brain disease involving compulsive substance use despite harmful consequences

concepts.intro: Alcohol is a depressant that impairs judgment, coordination, and reaction time, and its effects are especially harmful to the developing adolescent brain.
b: Alcohol impairs the frontal lobe first, affecting judgment and decision-making before physical coordination
Blood alcohol concentration (BAC) rises with each drink and is affected by body weight, sex, and how quickly alcohol is consumed
Binge drinking (4+ drinks for females, 5+ for males in about two hours) sharply raises the risk of alcohol poisoning
Alcohol poisoning can cause vomiting, unconsciousness, slowed breathing, and death; a person showing these signs needs emergency medical help
The teen brain, especially the prefrontal cortex, is still developing until the mid-20s, making it more vulnerable to alcohol's damaging effects
Long-term heavy alcohol use is linked to liver disease, certain cancers, and addiction

concepts.intro: Nicotine is a highly addictive stimulant found in cigarettes, e-cigarettes/vapes, and other tobacco products, and it is especially harmful to the developing adolescent brain.
b: Nicotine reaches the brain within seconds of inhalation and rapidly creates dependence, especially in teens
Vaping (e-cigarettes) delivers nicotine along with heated chemicals and flavorings; despite marketing, it is not a harmless alternative to smoking
Combustible cigarette smoke contains thousands of chemicals, including tar and carbon monoxide, and dozens of known carcinogens
Long-term tobacco use is the leading preventable cause of death in the U.S., linked to lung cancer, heart disease, and COPD
Nicotine exposure during adolescence can affect brain development related to attention, learning, and impulse control
Secondhand smoke exposes non-smokers to many of the same harmful chemicals

concepts.intro: Marijuana (cannabis) and other illicit drugs carry health and legal risks, and their effects vary widely by substance, dose, and the user's age.
b: THC, the main psychoactive compound in marijuana, affects memory, coordination, reaction time, and judgment
Regular marijuana use during adolescence is linked to impaired memory and learning, since the brain is still developing
Opioids (prescription painkillers and heroin) are highly addictive depressants that can cause fatal respiratory depression in overdose
Prescription drug misuse (taking medication not prescribed to you, or more than prescribed) carries the same risks as illegal drug use
Fentanyl, a powerful synthetic opioid, is increasingly mixed into other drugs, dramatically raising overdose risk even in small amounts
Naloxone (Narcan) can reverse an opioid overdose if administered quickly

concepts.l: Why People Use Substances and Risk/Protective Factors
concepts.intro: Understanding why people begin using substances helps identify effective prevention strategies, since risk rarely comes from a single cause.
b: Common risk factors include peer pressure, curiosity, stress, family history of addiction, and easy access to substances
Protective factors include strong family bonds, clear rules and expectations, positive peer groups, and involvement in school or extracurricular activities
Peer pressure can be direct (explicitly urging someone) or indirect (wanting to fit in without being asked)
Refusal skills — clearly saying no, suggesting an alternative, and being ready to leave a situation — reduce the likelihood of giving in to pressure
Media and advertising can normalize substance use, especially alcohol and vaping, through appealing imagery
Early use of any substance increases the statistical risk of developing dependence later in life

concepts.l: Addiction as a Disease and Paths to Recovery
concepts.intro: Addiction is recognized by medical science as a chronic disease of the brain's reward system, not a moral failing, and recovery is possible with proper treatment and support.
b: Addiction changes brain chemistry, particularly the dopamine reward pathway, reinforcing compulsive use despite negative consequences
Withdrawal symptoms occur when a physically dependent person stops using a substance, and can range from mild to medically dangerous
Effective treatment often combines behavioral therapy, support groups, and sometimes medication-assisted treatment
Relapse is common in recovery and does not mean treatment has failed; it often signals a need to adjust the treatment plan
Supportive, non-judgmental relationships significantly improve the likelihood of successful long-term recovery
Prevention programs that build refusal skills and healthy coping strategies reduce the likelihood of substance use starting in the first place

keyFacts: Nicotine reaches the brain within seconds and is highly addictive, especially for the developing teen brain
Binge drinking is defined as 4+ drinks for females or 5+ for males within about two hours
Fentanyl is a powerful synthetic opioid increasingly mixed into other drugs, greatly increasing overdose risk
Addiction is classified as a chronic brain disease affecting the dopamine reward system, not a moral failing
traps: Vaping is a harmless alternative to smoking, not true — vapes deliver addictive nicotine plus heated chemicals and are not proven safe
Marijuana is completely harmless because it's 'natural,' not true — THC impairs memory, coordination, and judgment, especially in the developing teen brain
Addiction is just a lack of willpower, not true — it is a chronic brain disease that changes the dopamine reward pathway and requires treatment
Prescription drugs are always safe because a doctor prescribes them, not true — taking them differently than prescribed or using someone else's prescription carries real risks

concepts.intro: Puberty is the biological process during which the body matures sexually and physically, triggered by hormones, and it brings physical, emotional, and social changes.
b: Puberty is triggered by increased production of hormones — estrogen and progesterone in females, testosterone in males
Physical changes in females include breast development, onset of menstruation, and growth spurts
Physical changes in males include voice deepening, facial/body hair growth, and growth spurts
Puberty typically begins between ages 8-13 in females and 9-14 in males, though timing varies widely and normally
Emotional changes during puberty include mood swings, increased self-consciousness, and a growing desire for independence
The brain, especially the prefrontal cortex responsible for judgment and impulse control, continues developing into the mid-20s

concepts.intro: The male and female reproductive systems each have specific organs and functions related to producing offspring, and understanding them is essential for making informed health decisions.
b: The female reproductive system includes the ovaries (produce eggs and hormones), fallopian tubes, uterus, and vagina
The menstrual cycle is roughly a 28-day hormonal cycle involving ovulation (egg release) and, if no fertilization occurs, menstruation
The male reproductive system includes the testes (produce sperm and testosterone), epididymis, vas deferens, and penis
Fertilization occurs when a sperm cell joins with an egg cell, typically in the fallopian tube
Regular check-ups and understanding one's own body are part of responsible reproductive health care
Both systems are regulated by hormones released from the brain's pituitary gland

concepts.intro: Pregnancy involves the development of a fertilized egg into a fetus over approximately 40 weeks, divided into three trimesters, each with distinct developmental milestones.
b: The first trimester (weeks 1-12) is when major organs and body systems begin to form, making it a critical period for avoiding harmful substances
The second trimester (weeks 13-27) involves rapid growth, and movement can typically be felt by the mother
The third trimester (weeks 28-40) is focused on continued growth and organ maturation in preparation for birth
Prenatal care (regular medical checkups during pregnancy) helps monitor the health of both mother and baby
Substances like alcohol, tobacco, and certain drugs can cause serious birth defects or developmental problems if used during pregnancy
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs) result from alcohol exposure during pregnancy and can cause lifelong physical and cognitive effects

concepts.intro: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections passed primarily through sexual contact, and understanding transmission and prevention is a core part of reproductive health education.
b: Common STIs include chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis, HPV, herpes, and HIV, each with different symptoms and treatments
Many STIs, especially chlamydia and HPV, often cause no symptoms, which is why regular testing is important for sexually active individuals
Abstinence (choosing not to have sex) is the only 100% effective method to prevent STIs and pregnancy
Condoms, when used correctly and consistently, significantly reduce (but do not eliminate) the risk of STI transmission
Untreated STIs can lead to serious complications, including infertility, and some (like HIV) are lifelong conditions
HPV vaccination can prevent infection with the strains of HPV most linked to cervical and other cancers

concepts.intro: Contraception refers to methods used to prevent pregnancy, and understanding the range of options — along with their effectiveness — supports informed, responsible decision-making.
b: Abstinence is the only method with zero risk of pregnancy or STI transmission from sexual contact
Barrier methods (like condoms) block sperm from reaching an egg and also reduce STI transmission risk
Hormonal methods (like birth control pills) prevent pregnancy by regulating hormones to prevent ovulation, but do not protect against STIs
No method other than abstinence is 100% effective at preventing pregnancy
Responsible decision-making includes considering physical, emotional, legal, and future-goal consequences before becoming sexually active
Open communication with a trusted adult or healthcare provider supports informed choices about reproductive health

concepts.l: Family Life, Parenting Readiness, and Life Stages
concepts.intro: Human development continues across the lifespan, and understanding the stages of life — along with the responsibilities of parenting — helps build realistic expectations for the future.
b: Erikson's stages of psychosocial development describe key challenges faced at each life stage, from infancy through late adulthood
Adolescence is a stage focused on identity development — figuring out values, goals, and a sense of self
Responsible parenting requires emotional maturity, financial stability, and a strong support system — readiness that most teens have not yet reached
Teen pregnancy carries increased health risks for both the parent and baby, and significant social and financial challenges
Healthy family relationships are built on communication, respect, and shared responsibilities
Life stages (infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, older adulthood) each bring distinct physical, cognitive, and social developmental tasks

keyFacts: Puberty is triggered by hormones — estrogen/progesterone in females and testosterone in males — and timing varies normally between individuals
Pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks, divided into three trimesters, each with distinct developmental milestones
Abstinence is the only method that is 100% effective at preventing both pregnancy and STI transmission
Many STIs, including chlamydia and HPV, often show no symptoms, making regular testing essential for sexually active people
traps: You can tell if someone has an STI just by looking at them, not true — many STIs show no visible symptoms at all
Birth control pills protect against STIs, not true — hormonal methods prevent pregnancy but provide no protection against sexually transmitted infections
Puberty happens at the exact same age and pace for everyone, not true — timing and pace vary widely and normally between individuals
A condom is 100% effective at preventing pregnancy and STIs, not true — used correctly it greatly reduces risk, but only abstinence is 100% effective
units.name: Human Development
Injury Prevention & Safety

concepts.l: Treating Common Injuries: RICE and Beyond
concepts.intro: Most sports and activity injuries — sprains, strains, and minor fractures — respond well to prompt, correct first aid, and knowing the difference between injury types determines the right response.
b: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament (connects bone to bone); a strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon (connects muscle to bone)
RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation — the standard first 24-48 hour treatment for most sprains and strains
Ice should be wrapped in a cloth, never applied directly to skin, and used for about 15-20 minutes at a time to avoid frostbite
Signs of a possible fracture include deformity, inability to bear weight, intense localized pain, and swelling — the area should be immobilized, not straightened
A person with a suspected head, neck, or spinal injury should not be moved unless there is immediate danger, since movement can worsen spinal damage
Applying heat is appropriate for muscle stiffness after the first 48 hours, not for a fresh injury, since heat increases swelling early on

concepts.l: CPR, AEDs, and Responding to Choking
concepts.intro: Cardiac arrest and choking are life-threatening emergencies where bystander action in the first few minutes dramatically affects survival, and basic steps can be learned by anyone.
b: The Cardiac Chain of Survival includes early recognition and calling 911, early CPR, early defibrillation (AED), and early advanced care
Hands-only CPR for an unresponsive adult who isn't breathing normally involves calling 911, then pushing hard and fast in the center of the chest at 100-120 compressions per minute
An AED (automated external defibrillator) talks the user through each step and will only deliver a shock if it detects a shockable heart rhythm
For a choking adult who cannot cough, speak, or breathe, abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich maneuver) are used to try to dislodge the object
Brain damage from lack of oxygen can begin within about 4-6 minutes, which is why calling 911 immediately and starting CPR without delay matters so much
Good Samaritan laws generally protect bystanders who provide reasonable emergency help in good faith from being sued if something goes wrong

concepts.intro: Motor vehicle crashes are the leading cause of death for U.S. teenagers, and most of the risk factors involved are preventable through specific behavior changes.
b: Seatbelts reduce the risk of fatal injury in a crash by roughly half and should be worn on every ride, including short trips
Distracted driving (texting, eating, adjusting music) slows reaction time similarly to driving impaired, even with hands-free devices
Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs impairs judgment, reaction time, and coordination, and is illegal at any measurable level for drivers under 21 in most states
Graduated driver's licensing (GDL) programs restrict new teen drivers' nighttime driving and number of passengers because both significantly raise crash risk
Pedestrians should cross at marked crosswalks, make eye contact with drivers, and stay visible (reflective clothing, lights) at night
Cyclists should wear a properly fitted helmet, ride with traffic flow, and use hand signals, since helmets significantly reduce the risk of serious head injury

concepts.intro: Environmental hazards like water, extreme heat, extreme cold, and severe weather cause preventable injuries and deaths every year, especially during outdoor recreation.
b: Drowning can happen silently and quickly, often without the splashing or shouting shown in movies, which is why constant, undistracted supervision near water matters
Never swim alone; swim in areas supervised by a lifeguard when possible, and always check current and rip current conditions before entering open water

Heat exhaustion (heavy sweating, weakness, nausea) can progress to heat stroke (high body temperature, confusion, hot/dry skin), which is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate cooling and 911
Hypothermia occurs when body temperature drops dangerously low from cold exposure, causing shivering, confusion, and slurred speech as it worsens
During lightning, the safest action is to get indoors or into a hard-topped vehicle; being in open fields, under trees, or in water are all high-risk locations
Wearing a properly fitted life jacket, rather than relying on swimming ability alone, is the most effective way to prevent drowning during boating

concepts.intro: Preventing violence — from bullying to weapons-related incidents — relies on recognizing warning signs early, defusing conflict, and knowing when and how to get help.
b: Bullying includes physical, verbal, social, and cyberbullying, and involves a repeated, intentional imbalance of power, not just a single disagreement
Bystanders who speak up, support the target, or report bullying to an adult significantly reduce how long bullying continues
De-escalation strategies include staying calm, using a non-threatening tone, giving the other person space, and walking away from an escalating situation when possible
Access to firearms is a major risk factor for both suicide and unintentional injury; a safely stored, unloaded firearm separate from ammunition significantly reduces this risk
Warning signs of a young person at risk for violence include sudden behavior changes, talk of hurting themselves or others, and social withdrawal
A home fire escape plan with two ways out of every room and a designated meeting spot should be practiced regularly, since most fatal home fires happen at night

concepts.l: Emergency Preparedness and the EMS System
concepts.intro: Knowing how to activate the emergency medical system (EMS) and prepare for likely local disasters turns a bystander into an effective first responder.
b: Calling 911 connects a caller to a dispatcher who can send police, fire, or EMS, and the caller should stay on the line and answer all questions calmly
Universal precautions — using gloves and avoiding contact with blood or bodily fluids — protect both the helper and the injured person from infection
A basic first aid kit should include bandages, gauze, antiseptic, tape, gloves, and any personal medications a family member needs
Disaster plans should be specific to regional risks (earthquake, tornado, hurricane, wildfire) and include an emergency kit with water, food, and a flashlight
The 'check, call, care' model — check the scene and victim for danger, call 911, then provide the care you're trained for — is the basic framework for any emergency response
Knowing your exact address and location is critical information to give a 911 dispatcher immediately, since responders cannot help if they can't find you

keyFacts: Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death among U.S. teenagers, and seatbelt use cuts fatal injury risk roughly in half
Hands-only CPR uses chest compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute for an unresponsive adult who isn't breathing normally
RICE (Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation) is the standard first 24-48 hour treatment for sprains and strains
Heat stroke — confusion with hot, dry skin and no sweating — is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate cooling and 911
traps: Hands-free texting or calls while driving are just as safe as not using a phone, not true — both divert attention and slow reaction time similarly to handheld use
You should always try to straighten or realign a suspected broken bone, not true — the area should be immobilized as found, not straightened
Applying ice directly to bare skin speeds healing, not true — direct ice contact for extended periods can cause frostbite; always use a cloth barrier
Drowning always looks dramatic, with lots of splashing and yelling, not true — it is often silent and quick, which is why constant supervision near water is essential

units.name: Disease Prevention

concepts.intro: Diseases fall into two broad categories based on whether they can spread from person to person, and the prevention strategy for each is very different.
b: Communicable (infectious) diseases are caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites) and can spread between people, like the flu or strep throat
Noncommunicable diseases are not spread from person to person and are usually caused by genetics, lifestyle, or environmental factors, like heart disease or type 2 diabetes
Chronic diseases (like heart disease and diabetes) develop and persist over a long period, while acute diseases (like a cold) come on quickly and resolve
Noncommunicable diseases account for the majority of deaths in the U.S., many of which are linked to preventable risk factors like smoking, inactivity, and poor diet
Some diseases, like certain cancers linked to HPV, blur the line by having an infectious cause but a noncommunicable, chronic course
Public health tracks disease patterns; an epidemic is a disease spreading rapidly in a specific area, while a pandemic is a global outbreak

concepts.l: How Pathogens Spread and the Immune System's Defense
concepts.intro: Understanding how pathogens travel from person to person, and how the immune system fights them off, explains why hygiene practices and vaccines work.
b: Pathogens spread through direct contact, respiratory droplets (coughing/sneezing), contaminated food or water, and vector-borne routes (like mosquitoes or ticks)
The body's first line of defense is physical barriers — skin, mucous membranes, and stomach acid — that block pathogens from entering
White blood cells are the immune system's second and third lines of defense, engulfing pathogens and producing antibodies that target specific invaders
Antibodies are proteins that recognize and bind to a specific pathogen, marking it for destruction and neutralizing it
After an infection, memory cells remain in the body, allowing a faster, stronger immune response if the same pathogen appears again
A fever is often a helpful immune response — raising body temperature makes the environment less favorable for many pathogens to reproduce

concepts.intro: Vaccines train the immune system to recognize a pathogen without causing the disease itself, and when enough of a population is vaccinated, it protects even those who cannot be.
b: A vaccine introduces a weakened, inactivated, or partial form of a pathogen (or instructions to build a piece of it) so the immune system builds memory cells without a real infection
Herd immunity occurs when a high enough percentage of a population is immune, which slows or stops disease spread and protects people who can't be vaccinated (infants, immunocompromised people)
Common childhood and adolescent vaccines protect against diseases like measles, whooping cough, HPV, and meningitis
Vaccines undergo extensive testing for safety and effectiveness before approval, and ongoing monitoring continues after release
Declining vaccination rates in a community can allow previously rare diseases, like measles, to reemerge in outbreaks
Vaccines do not cause the disease they protect against; mild, short-term side effects (soreness, low fever) are signs the immune system is responding, not signs of illness

concepts.l: Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer Risk Factors
concepts.intro: Cardiovascular disease and cancer are leading noncommunicable causes of death, and many of their risk factors are modifiable through lifestyle choices.
b: Cardiovascular disease includes conditions like heart disease and stroke, often caused by atherosclerosis — a buildup of plaque that narrows arteries
Modifiable cardiovascular risk factors include smoking, physical inactivity, poor diet, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol
Non-modifiable risk factors include age, family history, and genetics, which is why family health history matters even with a healthy lifestyle
Cancer occurs when cells grow and divide uncontrollably, and risk factors include tobacco use, excess UV exposure, certain infections (like HPV), and family history
Regular screenings (like skin checks, mammograms, or Pap tests as recommended by age) allow many cancers to be caught early, when treatment is most effective
Not all risk factors guarantee disease, and having no risk factors doesn't guarantee immunity — risk factors change probability, not certainty

concepts.intro: Many of the most common chronic diseases share the same small set of preventable lifestyle risk factors, which means the same healthy habits protect against multiple diseases at once.
b: Regular physical activity lowers the risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and some cancers
A diet high in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean protein — and lower in processed foods, added sugar, and sodium — reduces risk for multiple chronic diseases
Not smoking or vaping is one of the single most effective steps to reduce risk of cancer, heart disease, and lung disease
Managing stress and getting adequate sleep support immune function and reduce the physical toll linked to chronic disease
Type 2 diabetes, unlike type 1, is strongly linked to lifestyle factors like inactivity and excess body weight, and can often be prevented or delayed
Routine checkups allow a doctor to catch early warning signs (like rising blood pressure or blood sugar) before they become a diagnosed disease

concepts.intro: Simple, consistent hygiene habits break the chain of infection at the point of transmission and are among the most effective, low-cost tools for preventing communicable disease.
b: Washing hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially before eating and after using the bathroom, is one of the most effective ways to prevent illness
Covering a cough or sneeze with the elbow (not the hands) reduces the spread of respiratory droplets to surfaces and other people
Staying home when sick with a contagious illness protects others, especially those at higher risk like infants, older adults, and immunocompromised people
Properly cooking food to safe internal temperatures and refrigerating perishables promptly prevents foodborne illness from bacteria like Salmonella and E. coli
Not sharing personal items like water bottles, utensils, or towels reduces the spread of pathogens that live in saliva or on skin
Cleaning and disinfecting frequently touched surfaces (doorknobs, phones, desks) reduces the chance of picking up pathogens that survive outside the body

keyFacts: Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and spread between people; noncommunicable diseases are not spread person-to-person
Vaccines build immune memory using a weakened, inactivated, or partial pathogen so the body can respond quickly to a real future infection
Herd immunity protects people who cannot be vaccinated when enough of the surrounding population is immune
Handwashing with soap for at least 20 seconds is one of the single most effective ways to prevent the spread of illness
traps: Vaccines can give you the disease they protect against, not true — mild side effects like soreness or low fever are signs of an immune response, not illness
If you have no family history of a disease, lifestyle habits don't matter, not true — modifiable risk factors like diet, activity, and smoking affect risk regardless of genetics
Antibiotics work against viruses like the cold or flu, not true — antibiotics only treat bacterial infections, not viral ones
You can't spread an illness if you feel fine, not true — many pathogens are contagious during an incubation period before symptoms appear

units.name: Consumer & Community Health

concepts.intro: Health consumers are constantly targeted by advertising and health claims, and evaluating those claims critically protects both wallets and well-being.
b: Health fraud (quackery) involves selling products or services with false or exaggerated health claims, often targeting people desperate for a quick fix
Red flags for a health scam include promises of a 'miracle cure,' claims a product is suppressed by the medical establishment, and 'too good to be true' before-and-after results
Advertisers use techniques like testimonials, bandwagon appeals ('everyone's using it'), and appeals to fear or vanity to influence buying decisions
Checking a claim against a credible source (a doctor, the FDA, or a peer-reviewed study) before acting on it is a core critical-consumer skill
The FDA regulates the safety and labeling claims of food, drugs, and cosmetics, but dietary supplements are regulated far less strictly than medications
Comparing ingredients, cost per use, and independent reviews — rather than packaging or celebrity endorsement — leads to better health purchasing decisions

concepts.l: Understanding Health Insurance and Healthcare Costs
concepts.intro: Health insurance is a system for sharing the financial risk of medical costs, and understanding its basic vocabulary helps people make informed healthcare decisions.
b: A premium is the regular amount paid (often monthly) to have health insurance, regardless of whether care is used that month
A deductible is the amount a person must pay out-of-pocket for covered services before insurance starts paying its share
A copay is a fixed amount paid for a specific service (like a doctor's visit), while coinsurance is a percentage of the cost shared between patient and insurer
Preventive care (like annual checkups and many vaccines) is often covered at no additional cost because it catches problems early and reduces long-term costs
An emergency room visit is far more expensive than an urgent care or primary care visit and should be reserved for true emergencies
Being uninsured or underinsured can lead people to delay care, which often makes conditions more serious and more expensive to treat

concepts.intro: Different healthcare needs call for different types of providers and settings, and knowing which to use saves time, money, and gets more appropriate care.
b: A primary care provider manages overall health, routine checkups, and referrals to specialists when needed
Specialists (like a dermatologist or cardiologist) focus on a specific body system or condition and typically require a referral or specific need
Urgent care centers handle non-life-threatening issues that need prompt attention (minor cuts, infections), while emergency rooms are for life-threatening conditions
Mental health providers (counselors, therapists, psychiatrists) address emotional and psychological health, and psychiatrists specifically can prescribe medication
Checking a provider's credentials, reviews, and whether they're in-network with an insurance plan are practical steps before choosing care
Telehealth (virtual appointments) has expanded access to care, particularly for mental health and follow-up visits, though it isn't appropriate for every situation

concepts.l: Public Health Agencies and Their Roles
concepts.intro: A network of government agencies at the local, national, and global level works to protect community health through research, regulation, and response.
b: The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) tracks disease outbreaks, issues public health guidance, and conducts research on health threats within the U.S.
The FDA (Food and Drug Administration) regulates the safety of food, prescription and over-the-counter drugs, vaccines, and medical devices
The WHO (World Health Organization) coordinates global public health efforts, tracks disease across countries, and can declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern
Local and state health departments handle community-level needs: restaurant inspections, immunization clinics, and disease outbreak investigation
The EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) sets and enforces standards for air and water quality that directly affect community health
These agencies rely on data collection and surveillance to detect health trends early, allowing faster public health responses

concepts.intro: The environment where people live, work, and go to school directly shapes health outcomes, and communities can act collectively to reduce environmental health risks.
b: Air pollution (from vehicles, industry, or wildfire smoke) is linked to asthma, cardiovascular disease, and other respiratory conditions
Water quality standards, testing, and treatment protect communities from contaminants like lead and harmful bacteria
'Food deserts' are areas with limited access to affordable, healthy food, which is linked to poorer diet quality and higher chronic disease rates
Access to safe parks, sidewalks, and recreational spaces affects how much physical activity a community can realistically get
Environmental justice recognizes that pollution and health hazards are often unevenly distributed, disproportionately affecting lower-income communities
Community health resources like free clinics, food banks, and school-based health centers help fill gaps for people with limited access to care

concepts.l: Health Advocacy and Community Health Promotion
concepts.intro: Health advocacy means taking action to support health at a personal, community, or policy level, and it's a skill anyone can build regardless of age.
b: Advocacy can range from personal (asking a doctor clear questions) to community-level (organizing a health fair) to policy-level (supporting a public health law)
Health campaigns use messaging strategies — like clear calls to action and relatable messengers — to change community behavior (e.g., anti-vaping campaigns)
Peer health education, where trained students teach other students, is an effective way to spread accurate health information within a community
Being a credible advocate means using accurate, current information from reliable sources rather than opinion or rumor
Community health promotion efforts (immunization drives, mental health awareness weeks) work best when tailored to a community's specific needs and culture
Voting and civic engagement are also forms of health advocacy, since many policies (clean air rules, school lunch standards) directly affect public health

keyFacts: A premium is what you pay for insurance regardless of use; a deductible is what you pay out-of-pocket before insurance coverage kicks in
The CDC tracks disease and issues guidance nationally, the FDA regulates food/drug/device safety, and the WHO coordinates global public health
Dietary supplements are regulated far less strictly by the FDA than prescription or over-the-counter medications
Urgent care is for prompt, non-life-threatening issues; the emergency room is reserved for life-threatening conditions
traps: 'Natural' or 'FDA-approved' on a supplement label guarantees it's safe and effective, not true — supplements face much lighter regulation than medications
Going to the ER for any medical concern is always the right call, not true — non-emergencies are better and more affordably handled at urgent care or a primary provider
A higher premium always means better coverage, not true — plans vary widely in deductibles, copays, and networks, so total cost depends on the whole plan
Public health agencies only matter during a crisis, not true — they do ongoing work like restaurant inspections, immunization programs, and water quality monitoring year-round

units.name: Healthy Relationships

concepts.l: Characteristics of Healthy vs. Unhealthy Relationships
concepts.intro: All relationships — friendships, family, and romantic — fall somewhere on a spectrum from healthy to unhealthy to abusive, and recognizing the pattern matters more than any single incident.
b: Healthy relationships are built on mutual respect, trust, honesty, equality, and support for each person's individuality and other relationships
Unhealthy relationships often involve some controlling behavior, dishonesty, or disrespect, but haven't escalated to abuse
Warning signs of an unhealthy dynamic include extreme jealousy, checking a partner's phone without permission, and pressuring someone to change who they spend time with
A healthy relationship allows both people to maintain outside friendships and interests rather than expecting one person to meet all social needs
Respecting a partner's or friend's boundaries — even when you disagree with them — is a core sign of a healthy relationship
Relationships can shift between healthy and unhealthy over time; noticing the shift early makes it easier to address

concepts.intro: Conflict is a normal part of any relationship; what determines whether a relationship stays healthy is how the people involved communicate through it.
b: Active listening means fully focusing on the speaker, not planning your response while they're talking, and reflecting back what you heard
'I' statements (e.g., 'I feel frustrated when...') express a concern without blaming, which reduces defensiveness compared to 'you' statements
Nonverbal communication — tone, facial expression, body language — often carries as much meaning as the words being said
Healthy conflict resolution focuses on the specific issue at hand rather than bringing up unrelated past grievances or attacking the other person's character
Compromise means both people give a little to reach a solution both can accept, rather than one person always winning the disagreement
Taking a short break when a conversation gets too heated, then returning to it calmly, prevents conflicts from escalating into harmful arguments

concepts.intro: Boundaries are the limits a person sets for what they are and are not comfortable with, and consent is the clear, ongoing agreement required before any shared activity, especially physical intimacy.
b: A boundary can be physical, emotional, or digital (like not sharing private messages), and healthy relationships respect all three
Consent must be freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic, and specific (sometimes remembered as F.R.I.E.S.)
Consent to one activity is not consent to another, and consent given once is not consent for every future time
A person who is asleep, unconscious, or impaired by alcohol or drugs cannot legally or ethically give consent
Silence or the absence of 'no' is not the same as a 'yes' — clear, active agreement is required
Communicating boundaries clearly and directly, and respecting them when someone else states theirs, is a learnable skill that strengthens trust

concepts.intro: Abuse in a relationship can be physical, emotional, sexual, or digital, and recognizing early warning signs — in your own relationship or a friend's — is critical to getting help before harm escalates.
b: Physical abuse involves hitting, pushing, or any physical harm; emotional abuse involves manipulation, humiliation, isolation, or threats
Digital abuse includes constant monitoring, demanding passwords, or pressuring someone through texts and social media
The cycle of abuse often includes a tension-building phase, an incident, then a 'honeymoon' phase of apology and calm — which can make leaving feel confusing or difficult
Warning signs in a friend's relationship include isolation from friends and family, unexplained injuries, extreme secrecy, or sudden personality changes
Leaving an abusive relationship is often the most dangerous time, so safety planning with a trusted adult, counselor, or hotline is important rather than acting alone
The National Domestic Violence Hotline and school counselors are confidential resources available to anyone in or worried about an abusive relationship

concepts.intro: Peers strongly influence adolescent decision-making, and assertive communication is the key skill that allows someone to stay true to their values under social pressure.
b: Peer pressure can be positive (encouraging healthy habits) or negative (pushing risky behavior), and it can be direct (explicitly urging) or indirect (implied expectation)
Assertive communication expresses your own needs and opinions clearly and respectfully, without being passive (avoiding conflict at your own expense) or aggressive (disrespecting others)
Refusal skills include saying no clearly, offering an alternative, using humor to deflect, and being willing to leave a situation
Having at least one planned exit strategy (a text code word, a ride arranged in advance) makes it easier to leave an uncomfortable situation without confrontation
Surrounding yourself with peers who share your values reduces the frequency and intensity of negative peer pressure you'll face
Assertiveness is a skill that improves with practice, and role-playing difficult conversations in advance builds confidence to use it in the moment

concepts.intro: Family relationships, whatever form they take, are often a person's first and most enduring support system, and the same principles of healthy communication apply within them.
b: Families take many forms — nuclear, single-parent, blended, extended, or chosen family — and healthy family function depends on the relationships within it, not its structure
Healthy family communication includes expressing needs directly, listening without immediately reacting, and resolving conflict without contempt or stonewalling
Adolescence often includes natural friction with parents/guardians as teens seek more independence, which is a normal developmental process, not a sign of family failure
A strong support system — family, friends, mentors, or community — is one of the most protective factors for mental health and resilience through difficult times
Setting appropriate boundaries with family members (like privacy or personal space) can be done respectfully while still maintaining closeness
When family conflict becomes severe or unsafe, school counselors, family therapists, or trusted adults outside the family can provide support and mediation

keyFacts: Consent must be freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic, and specific — often remembered with the acronym F.R.I.E.S.
The cycle of abuse typically includes tension-building, an incident, and a 'honeymoon' reconciliation phase, which can make leaving feel confusing
Assertive communication expresses your needs clearly and respectfully, distinct from passive (avoiding conflict) or aggressive (disrespecting others) styles
'I' statements reduce defensiveness in conflict by expressing a feeling without directly blaming the other person
traps: If someone doesn't say 'no,' that means they've consented, not true — consent requires clear, active, enthusiastic agreement, not just the absence of refusal
Jealousy is proof that a partner really cares, not true — extreme jealousy and controlling behavior are warning signs of an unhealthy or abusive dynamic, not love
Leaving an abusive relationship is simple once you decide to do it, not true — leaving is often the most dangerous period, which is why safety planning with help matters
Arguing means a relationship is failing, not true — conflict is normal in any relationship; what matters is whether it's handled with respect and resolution

quiz.q: Which is a core characteristic of a healthy relationship?
o: Mutual respect and trust between both people
One partner making all the decisions
Expecting your partner to give up other friendships
Checking your partner's phone without permission
quiz.e: Healthy relationships are built on mutual respect, trust, honesty, and equality, with room for each person's individuality.

quiz.q: Which behavior is a warning sign of an unhealthy relationship?
o: Encouraging a partner to keep close friendships and outside interests
Extreme jealousy and controlling who a partner spends time with
Respecting a partner's need for personal space and alone time
Compromising calmly during a disagreement about weekend plans
quiz.e: Extreme jealousy and controlling behavior are early warning signs of an unhealthy dynamic, not signs of caring.

quiz.q: What does an 'I' statement do in a conflict?
o: Lists the other person's mistakes so they understand the problem
Ends the discussion quickly so that no one feels pressured
Expresses a feeling without directly blaming the other person
Demands that the other person apologize before anything else
quiz.e: 'I' statements like 'I feel frustrated when...' reduce defensiveness compared to accusatory 'you' statements.

quiz.q: What is active listening?
o: Fully focusing on the speaker instead of planning your response
Waiting for a pause so you can share your own opinion quickly
Doing a second task while still catching the main points
Agreeing with the speaker to avoid conflict during the conversation
quiz.e: Active listening means giving full attention and reflecting back what was heard, rather than mentally preparing a rebuttal.

quiz.q: What does the F in the F.R.I.E.S. consent model stand for?
o: Freely given
Forceful
Final
Formal
quiz.e: F.R.I.E.S. stands for Freely given, Reversible, Informed, Enthusiastic, and Specific.

quiz.q: Which statement about consent is TRUE?
o: Silence or a lack of resistance can count as agreement
Consent given once in a relationship carries over to later occasions
Agreement given after repeated pressure still counts as consent
Consent to one activity is not automatic consent to another
quiz.e: Consent must be specific to each activity and each time; it can never be assumed from silence or a past agreement.

quiz.q: A boundary in a relationship can be which of the following?
o: Physical but not emotional
Physical, emotional, or digital
Emotional, not physical or digital
Set by parents rather than teens
quiz.e: Boundaries can be physical, emotional, or digital (such as not sharing private messages), and healthy relationships respect all three.

quiz.q: Which best describes emotional abuse?
o: Physical violence that leaves visible injuries on a partner
A single heated disagreement followed by a sincere apology
Honest feedback shared respectfully about a partner's behavior
Manipulation, humiliation, isolation, or threats
quiz.e: Emotional abuse involves manipulation, humiliation, isolating someone from support, or making threats, without necessarily involving physical harm.

quiz.q: What is the 'honeymoon phase' in the cycle of abuse?
o: The early stage when a new healthy relationship first begins
A stage of rising tension before any abusive incident happens
A period of apology and calm following an abusive incident
A counseling session where both partners agree to share blame
quiz.e: The cycle of abuse often includes tension-building, an incident, then a honeymoon phase of apology and calm, which can make leaving feel confusing.

quiz.q: Why is leaving an abusive relationship often dangerous?
o: The risk of harm can increase right when someone tries to leave
Abusive partners usually calm down and become safer once someone leaves
The danger ends the moment a person makes the decision to leave
Abuse fades on its own once enough time passes in the relationship
quiz.e: Leaving is often the most dangerous period in an abusive relationship, which is why safety planning with a trusted adult or hotline matters.

quiz.q: Which resource offers confidential help for someone worried about an abusive relationship?
o: A post on public social media asking followers for advice
A group chat with classmates who know both people involved
The National Domestic Violence Hotline or a school counselor
A tabloid advice column or an online comment section
quiz.e: The National Domestic Violence Hotline and school counselors are confidential resources available to anyone in or concerned about an abusive relationship.

quiz.q: What distinguishes assertive communication from aggressive communication?
o: Assertive communication avoids stating needs to keep everyone comfortable and calm
Assertive communication pushes your needs forward by overpowering the other person
Assertive communication respects others while clearly stating your own needs
Assertive communication means hinting at wants and hoping others notice them
quiz.e: Assertive communication expresses your needs clearly and respectfully, unlike aggressive communication, which disrespects others.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a refusal skill?
o: Saying no clearly and offering an alternative
Giving in to avoid an awkward moment
Ignoring the pressure and hoping it stops
Pretending you don't understand the request
quiz.e: Refusal skills include saying no directly, suggesting an alternative, and being willing to leave the situation if needed.

quiz.q: What is an example of indirect peer pressure?
o: A friend openly telling you to try something so you can join in
Being offered a dare by classmates who ask you to go along
A friend threatening to stop talking to you unless you take part
Feeling like you must act a certain way because 'everyone else does'
quiz.e: Indirect peer pressure comes from an implied expectation to fit in, rather than someone explicitly urging a behavior.

quiz.q: How can family structure affect healthy family functioning?
o: Families with two married parents function well because that structure ensures stability
Healthy function depends on the relationships within the family, not its structure
Blended families with stepparents tend to be unstable because of their structure
Extended families with grandparents at home often lack the privacy needed to function well
quiz.e: Families take many forms, and healthy functioning depends on communication and respect within the relationships, not the family's structure.

quiz.q: Why might friction increase between teens and parents during adolescence?
o: The family is failing, since arguments signal serious dysfunction at home
Teens are naturally seeking more independence, a normal developmental process
Teens no longer need parental guidance or support once they reach adolescence
Parents have become less caring, which causes teens to push back
quiz.e: Increased friction as teens seek independence is a normal part of adolescent development, not necessarily a sign of family dysfunction.

quiz.q: What is a healthy way to handle conflict that is becoming too heated?
o: Keep arguing until one person finally gives in and concedes
Bring up unrelated past arguments to prove your point
Stop speaking to the person for several weeks to make a point
Take a short break, then return to the conversation calmly
quiz.e: Taking a short break and returning calmly prevents conflicts from escalating into harmful arguments.

quiz.q: What does compromise mean in resolving a disagreement?
o: One person gives in to the other's demands to end the argument quickly
Both people stop talking about the issue and agree to disagree for good
The stronger or louder person decides the outcome for the group
Both people give a little to reach a solution they can both accept
quiz.e: Compromise means both people adjust their position somewhat to reach a mutually acceptable solution.

quiz.q: Which is a sign that a friend may be in an unhealthy or abusive relationship?
o: Increasing isolation from friends and family, and unexplained injuries
Spending time regularly with a wide group of friends and family
Talking openly about disagreements with their partner and resolving them
Keeping hobbies and activities outside of the relationship going strong
quiz.e: Isolation from a support network, unexplained injuries, and extreme secrecy are common warning signs of an abusive relationship.

quiz.q: Why is having a planned exit strategy useful in an uncomfortable social situation?
o: It helps you persuade others to change their plans
It lets you confront the people pressuring you directly
It provides a way to leave without confrontation
It helps you avoid the people involved in the future
quiz.e: A planned exit strategy, like a pre-arranged ride or code word, makes it easier to leave an uncomfortable situation without a scene.

quiz.q: What role does nonverbal communication play in a conversation?
o: It has little effect on how a message is understood
It matters mainly in formal settings like interviews or speeches
It can carry as much meaning as the words spoken
It reliably matches the words, so it adds no new information
quiz.e: Tone, facial expression, and body language often carry as much meaning as the words themselves.

quiz.q: Which best defines digital abuse in a relationship?
o: Occasionally texting a partner to check in after practice
Sharing a photo publicly on a personal social media account
Both partners agreeing to share one streaming account
Constant monitoring or demanding a partner's passwords
quiz.e: Digital abuse includes constant monitoring, demanding passwords, or pressuring someone through texts and social media.

quiz.q: Can a person who is impaired by alcohol give consent?
o: Yes, as long as the person is still able to talk and walk
Yes, if the person said yes earlier in the evening before drinking
No, impairment prevents someone from legally or ethically giving consent
Yes, provided the person is the one who initiated the contact
quiz.e: A person who is asleep, unconscious, or impaired by alcohol or drugs cannot legally or ethically give consent.

quiz.q: What is one benefit of surrounding yourself with peers who share your values?
o: It prevents negative peer pressure from occurring in your friendships
It replaces the need for personal boundaries and refusal skills
It reduces the frequency and intensity of negative peer pressure
It makes you more likely to follow the group when values conflict
quiz.e: Peers who share your values create an environment with less negative pressure to act against your own judgment.

quiz.q: What is one protective factor for mental health during difficult times?
o: A strong support system of family, friends, or mentors
Withdrawing from close relationships to avoid being a burden
Keeping personal problems private rather than sharing them with others
Relying on yourself rather than asking for any outside help
quiz.e: A strong support system is one of the most protective factors for mental health and resilience through difficult times.

quiz.q: How should healthy conflict resolution address past issues?
o: Bring up earlier disagreements to show a pattern of behavior
Focus on the specific current issue rather than past grievances
Set aside the present problem and revisit old arguments first
Decide who is at fault by counting past mistakes on each side
quiz.e: Healthy conflict resolution stays focused on the issue at hand rather than dragging in unrelated past grievances.

quiz.q: Which of these is considered physical abuse?
o: Hitting, pushing, or any physical harm to a partner
Disagreeing about plans for the weekend with a partner
Setting a boundary about personal space and alone time
Taking a short break from an argument to cool down
quiz.e: Physical abuse involves hitting, pushing, or any form of physical harm, distinguishing it from normal relationship conflict.

quiz.q: Why is respecting someone's stated boundary important, even if you disagree with it?
o: It matters in romantic relationships but not among friends or family
It is optional when you believe the boundary is unreasonable
It is a core sign of a healthy relationship and builds trust
It ensures the other person will agree with you later on
quiz.e: Respecting a partner's or friend's boundaries, even when you disagree, is a core sign of a healthy relationship.

quiz.q: What can help de-escalate family conflict that becomes severe or unsafe?
o: Waiting for tempers to cool and the conflict to pass
Support from a school counselor or family therapist
Taking sides with the family member who seems most upset
Posting about the conflict online to gather opinions
quiz.e: School counselors, family therapists, or other trusted adults outside the family can provide support and mediation for severe family conflict.

quiz.q: Which is an example of positive peer influence?
o: A friend pressuring you to skip class and hang out
A classmate daring you to try something risky for fun
A group making you feel left out unless you change your values
A friend encouraging you to study or exercise regularly
quiz.e: Peer pressure can be positive when it encourages healthy habits, not just negative when it pushes risky behavior.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between passive communication and personal needs?
o: Passive communication states your needs firmly while respecting others' views
Passive communication demands that your needs be met by overriding other people
Passive communication avoids conflict at the expense of expressing your own needs
Passive communication shares needs openly but ignores how others feel
quiz.e: Passive communication avoids conflict but often means your own needs and opinions go unexpressed.

quiz.q: Consent that is 'reversible' means what?
o: A person must keep going once an activity has started
A person can change their mind before an activity begins, not during it
A person's agreement carries over automatically to future activities
A person can change their mind at any point, even mid-activity
quiz.e: Reversible consent means a person can withdraw agreement at any time, even during an activity they initially agreed to.

quiz.q: Which best describes chosen family?
o: A group of biological relatives who live together in one home
A legal arrangement formed when a child is adopted by a family
A household of two parents and their children living together
A close support network of people not related by blood or marriage
quiz.e: Chosen family refers to close, family-like support networks made up of people not necessarily related by blood or marriage.

quiz.q: What should you do if a friend shows signs of being in an abusive relationship?
o: Express concern and help connect them with a trusted adult or resource
Confront the partner directly and demand that they stop
Stay out of it because other people's relationships are private
Share what you've seen in a public post to pressure the partner
quiz.e: Expressing concern privately and helping a friend connect with a trusted adult or hotline is safer and more supportive than confrontation or public exposure.

quiz.q: Why does adolescence often involve seeking more independence from parents?
o: It is a normal part of healthy development
It signals the parent-child bond is weakening
It usually signals underlying conflict at home
It is a phase parents should work to prevent
quiz.e: Seeking independence during adolescence is a normal developmental process, not a sign that the family relationship is failing.

quiz.q: What makes consent 'enthusiastic' under the F.R.I.E.S. model?
o: It reflects agreement given after repeated asking by a partner
It means agreement that was given once and lasts through the relationship
It reflects the absence of a clear no rather than a clear yes
It reflects genuine, willing agreement rather than reluctant compliance
quiz.e: Enthusiastic consent means genuine willingness, not just an absence of objection or reluctant agreement.

quiz.q: How can practicing role-play conversations help with assertiveness?
o: It replaces the need to ever have the real conversation
It builds confidence to use assertive skills in real situations
It ensures the other person will respond the way you rehearsed
It works for adults but is not useful for teens learning skills
quiz.e: Rehearsing difficult conversations in advance builds confidence to be assertive when the real situation happens.

quiz.q: What is one sign that a relationship may be shifting from healthy to unhealthy?
o: One partner increasingly discourages outside friendships
Both partners keep up their own hobbies and friend groups
The partners work through disagreements calmly and respectfully
Each partner respects the other's stated boundaries and space
quiz.e: A shift toward discouraging outside friendships and increasing control is a sign a relationship may be becoming unhealthy.

quiz.q: Why is it important to notice early warning signs of an unhealthy relationship?
o: Early behaviors usually fade by themselves, so waiting is the better approach
Early warning signs usually reflect a one-time mistake, not a lasting pattern
Addressing issues early makes them easier to resolve before they escalate
Noticing early signs matters mainly to decide who is at fault for the problem
quiz.e: Relationships can shift between healthy and unhealthy over time, and noticing early makes it easier to address the shift.

quiz.q: What is the safest first step if you're unsure whether your own relationship is unhealthy?
o: Talk to a trusted adult, counselor, or hotline for guidance
Wait several months to see whether the behavior changes by itself
Confront the partner right away and demand that the behavior stop
Ask friends online whether the behavior is normal in relationships
quiz.e: Talking with a trusted adult, school counselor, or a confidential hotline is a safe way to get guidance about relationship concerns.

quiz.q: Which best describes the mental health continuum?
o: A two-category label that sorts people as either healthy or mentally ill
A single score assigned at diagnosis that stays the same over time
A range from thriving to struggling that people move along over time
A scale of treatment stages for people with a diagnosed disorder
quiz.e: Mental health is dynamic and exists on a continuum influenced by risk and protective factors.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a protective factor for mental health?
o: Chronic sleep deprivation
A strong, supportive friendship
Social isolation
Untreated chronic stress
quiz.e: Supportive relationships are one of the strongest protective factors against poor mental health.

quiz.q: What triggers the 'fight-or-flight' response?
o: A rise in insulin and melatonin after a large meal
The release of adrenaline and cortisol in response to a perceived threat
The release of serotonin and oxytocin during relaxing social contact
A drop in body temperature and heart rate during deep sleep
quiz.e: The stress response releases adrenaline and cortisol to prepare the body to react to a threat.

quiz.q: What is 'eustress'?
o: Long-lasting stress that damages health and weakens immunity
Short-term stress that triggers a fight-or-flight response
Positive stress that can motivate and improve performance
A clinical anxiety disorder requiring professional treatment
quiz.e: Eustress is short-term, positive stress, like nervous excitement before a performance or game.

quiz.q: Chronic stress is most closely linked to which physical effect?
o: Stronger immune function and lower blood pressure
Weakened immune function and high blood pressure
Faster digestion and improved absorption of nutrients
Sharper memory and a lower resting heart rate
quiz.e: Long-term elevated cortisol from chronic stress can weaken immunity and raise blood pressure.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a healthy coping strategy?
o: Talking to a trusted friend or adult about the stressor
Putting off the problem for as long as possible
Using alcohol or other substances to dull the feeling
Withdrawing from friends and family until it passes
quiz.e: Talking through stress with someone trustworthy is a healthy, effective coping strategy.

quiz.q: What does 'self-awareness' mean in emotional intelligence?
o: Understanding what other people are feeling
Choosing how to respond when you feel upset
Motivating yourself to reach long-term goals
Accurately recognizing and naming what you feel
quiz.e: Self-awareness is accurately identifying your own emotions and their triggers.

quiz.q: Empathy is best defined as:
o: Agreeing with another person's choices and opinions
Feeling sorry for another person from a safe distance
Controlling your own emotions during a conversation
Understanding and sharing another person's feelings
quiz.e: Empathy means genuinely understanding and sharing in another's emotional experience.

quiz.q: How long must symptoms of low mood and loss of interest persist to be diagnosed as depression?
o: A few hours
One day
Two weeks or more
One year minimum
quiz.e: Clinical depression requires symptoms lasting two weeks or longer that interfere with daily life.

quiz.q: Generalized anxiety disorder is characterized by:
o: Short bursts of nervousness tied to a specific test or event
Excessive, hard-to-control worry most days for six months or more
Sudden, intense panic attacks that peak within about ten minutes
Intrusive thoughts and repetitive rituals that take over daily routines
quiz.e: GAD involves persistent, excessive worry that is difficult to control and interferes with daily life.

quiz.q: Which is considered an unhealthy coping mechanism?
o: Deep breathing exercises
Physical activity
Substance use to escape feelings
Talking to a school counselor
quiz.e: Substance use provides short-term relief but worsens problems and does not address the root cause.

quiz.q: Resilience is best described as:
o: The ability to stay calm by avoiding stressful moments
A fixed trait that is set in early childhood
The ability to adapt and recover after setbacks
Feeling no sadness or stress when problems arise
quiz.e: Resilience is a learnable skill involving adaptation and recovery from adversity.

quiz.q: Which factor most strongly builds resilience?
o: A high level of intelligence and academic achievement
A strong support network of family, friends, or mentors
Avoiding difficult situations so that stress stays low
A strict routine that limits exposure to unexpected change
quiz.e: Supportive relationships are one of the biggest predictors of resilience.

quiz.q: What is cognitive reframing?
o: Pushing a stressful situation out of mind so that it stops mattering
Changing how you interpret a stressful situation to reduce its emotional impact
Taking full blame for a stressful situation to feel more in control
Distracting yourself with activities until the situation goes away
quiz.e: Reframing shifts your perspective on a situation to make it feel more manageable.

quiz.q: Which is a warning sign of possible suicide risk?
o: Increased interest in future plans
